story.headline: Oil gave back an early jump after the US let some blacklisted tankers unload, leaving most currencies flat. The pound held near $1.34 on hot UK inflation, and France's 10-year borrowing cost topped 5%.

reads.policy: Britain's hot inflation figure all but settles a Bank of England hike in November, and Australian hike bets kept rising. Canada and New Zealand are also expected to raise rates next week, while the Fed waits until December. Currencies whose central banks are about to act keep the rate edge.
reads.growth: US housing stays weak under high mortgage rates, and UK house prices grew at their slowest pace since March. None of it moved rate bets today, because central banks are watching inflation, not growth.
reads.inflation: UK inflation rose more than expected as fuel costs fed through, and German producer prices also ran hot, so the oil shock is still lifting prices. That keeps central banks leaning toward hikes. Coming up: New Zealand's inflation report at 4:45 PM CT tonight and Japan's on Thursday evening.
reads.risk: Iran's hard line and more US warships raised tension in the Gulf, but markets stayed calm and safe-haven currencies got no extra lift. The real stress point is France, where borrowing costs hit their highest in more than 20 years.
reads.tot: Oil rose in the morning and gave it back after Washington moved to ease supply, ending near $109. Prices that high still help exporters like Canada and cost importers like Japan, the euro area and Britain. Europe's gas bill climbed too.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds are betting most heavily against the Canadian dollar, even as a Bank of Canada hike looks likely, which leaves those bets exposed if the loonie keeps rising. They also bet against the kiwi and the euro. In the yen and the Aussie, hedge funds and long-term investors take opposite sides.
reads.fiscal: France's borrowing costs rose above 5%, a sign investors want more to hold French debt before Moody's review on Friday and a budget vote on October 27. In Britain, borrowing ran above forecast a week before the budget, leaving less room for help with energy bills.

fed.summary: The Fed is expected to hold rates on October 28 and raise them in December, because high oil is keeping inflation up. That keeps US rates the highest among the big economies and supports the dollar.
fed.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike very likely.
fed.why: Energy-driven inflation is still too high for the Fed's comfort, even as the housing market weakens under high mortgage rates.
fed.watch: Weekly jobless claims on Thursday and whether oil stays high enough to keep the December hike alive; the Fed is in its quiet period until October 28.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada is expected to raise rates on October 28, after Governor Tiff Macklem warned that energy will push its inflation forecast substantially higher. Most of that hike is already in the loonie's price.
boc.why: Higher energy prices are lifting Canada's inflation outlook, and the bank has signalled it will not let that slide.
boc.watch: Canadian producer prices on Thursday, and whether oil holds up into the decision; a surprise hold would hit the loonie.

rbnz.summary: New Zealand's central bank is leaning toward a rate hike on October 28. Tonight's inflation report decides whether it goes ahead.
rbnz.priced: October 28: hike likely; December: second hike a coin toss.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the bank's target, and strong business activity and firmer dairy prices give it room to act.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand's third-quarter inflation report at 4:45 PM CT tonight; a clearly soft figure would revive talk of a hold.

ecb.summary: The ECB is set to hold on October 29 and is leaning toward a hike in December, as euro-area inflation runs near twice its goal. France's rising borrowing costs complicate the picture for the euro.
ecb.priced: October 29: hold expected; December: hike likely.
ecb.why: Expensive energy keeps euro-area inflation well above target, while France's budget trouble adds a financial-stress risk.
ecb.watch: Moody's review of France on Friday and the French revenue vote on October 27, ahead of the decision.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan is expected to hold on October 30 and raise rates in December, as officials say underlying inflation is close to 2%. That gives the yen some support against a wide gap with US rates.
boj.priced: October 30: hold expected; December: hike likely.
boj.why: Officials say underlying inflation is nearing the 2% goal and borrowing conditions are still easy, which argues for gradual hikes.
boj.watch: Japan's national inflation figures on Thursday evening CT, and whether the bank lifts its inflation forecasts next week.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised rates four times this year, and officials' warnings on sticky inflation have revived talk of a fifth hike in November. That has lifted the Aussie to a three-week high.
rba.priced: November 3: hike possible, a bit less than even odds; December: hike more likely than not.
rba.why: Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser says the inflation outlook has worsened, partly because of oil, and the bank is unsure rates are high enough.
rba.watch: Australia's third-quarter inflation report on October 28, the number that settles November.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is all but certain to raise rates on November 5, its first hike in years, after UK inflation jumped to 3.5%. That keeps UK rates high and supports the pound.
boe.priced: November 5: hike near certain; December: second hike a coin toss.
boe.why: Energy costs are pushing UK inflation well above the 2% target, and pay and services prices are still rising fast.
boe.watch: The UK budget on October 28 and any hints from policymakers about a second hike in December.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank is holding rates at zero and could even cut in December, because Swiss inflation is very low. The franc moves more on global fear than on Swiss news.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is close to zero and the strong franc keeps import prices down, so the bank has no reason to tighten.
snb.watch: The SNB's summary of its September policy discussion on Thursday, for how worried it is about the strong franc.

USD.summary: The dollar sits near a three-week low but still holds the highest rates among the majors, with a Fed hike expected in December because oil keeps inflation high.

notes.policy: The Fed is expected to hold in October and hike in December, keeping US rates the highest of the majors.
notes.inflation: High oil keeps US inflation well above the Fed's goal, which supports the case for more hikes.

EUR.summary: The euro is held back by France's rising borrowing costs and Europe's energy bill, even though the ECB leans toward a December hike.

notes.policy: The ECB is expected to hike only once, in December, while others move sooner, so the euro's rate edge is thin.
notes.growth: Euro-area growth is weak under high energy costs, which limits how far rates can rise.
notes.inflation: Inflation near twice the ECB's goal keeps a December hike likely, which helps the euro.
notes.tot: Europe imports most of its energy, so oil and gas near their highs drain money out of the euro area.
notes.fiscal: France's borrowing costs rose above 5% before a Moody's review, keeping a budget risk on the euro.

GBP.summary: The pound is one of the stronger currencies, because hot UK inflation and a firm jobs market make a Bank of England hike in November almost certain.

notes.policy: A November Bank of England hike is near certain and a second in December is a coin toss, which keeps UK rates high.
notes.growth: Britain's jobs market is holding up better than expected, which gives the Bank room to hike.
notes.inflation: UK inflation jumped to 3.5% on energy, well above target, pushing the Bank toward higher rates.

JPY.summary: The yen stays weak near 158 per dollar because US rates are far higher and Japan pays more for imported energy, though a December Bank of Japan hike offers some support.

notes.policy: Even with a December hike likely, Japan's rates stay far below US rates, which keeps the yen soft.
notes.tot: Japan imports almost all its energy, so high oil widens its trade gap and weighs on the yen.

CHF.summary: The franc is firm because investors park money there when the Gulf and France look shaky, not because of anything Swiss.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is very low, so the SNB may cut in December, which works against the franc.
notes.risk: Worry about the Gulf war and France's debt sends money into the franc as a safe place to wait.

AUD.summary: The Aussie is at a three-week high because the RBA keeps warning about sticky inflation and a November hike is back on the table.

notes.policy: RBA officials are openly weighing a fifth hike, which keeps Australian rates among the highest of the majors.
notes.growth: Australia's job market is cooling, which could make the RBA more careful.
notes.tot: Australia sells commodities abroad, so firm prices for its exports bring money in.

CAD.summary: The loonie is near its strongest in a month because a Bank of Canada hike on October 28 is close to fully priced and oil, Canada's main export, stays high.

notes.policy: A Bank of Canada hike next week looks very likely, which lifts Canadian rates.
notes.growth: Canada's economy has been losing jobs, which is a weak spot for the loonie.
notes.tot: High oil prices bring more money into Canada, its biggest export.

NZD.summary: The kiwi is waiting on tonight's inflation report, which decides whether New Zealand's central bank raises rates on October 28.

notes.policy: A rate hike on October 28 is likely, which supports the kiwi if inflation cooperates.
notes.growth: Business activity in New Zealand is running strong, backing the case for higher rates.
notes.risk: A calm global mood helps the kiwi, which tends to rise when investors feel confident.
notes.tot: Firmer dairy prices, New Zealand's main export, bring more money into the country.
